Method: Fourier entropy versus total influence exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: Discarding the Boolean constraint destroys the claim: the probability measure uniform on the n singleton subsets has entropy log2(n) but mean subset size1. It cannot be the squared spectrum of a Boolean function when n>=2. Check: If all Fourier mass were on singletons, f=sum_i a_i*x_i with a_i=plus/minus1/sqrt(n). In f^2 the coefficient of x_i*x_j is2*a_i*a_j, nonzero for distinct i,j, whereas Boolean f requires f^2=1. This independently exhibits the violated Fourier convolution identity. Obstruction: Entropy versus mean cardinality alone is insufficient. Any proof must use the nonlinear identities imposed by f^2=1; no dimension-free inequality exploiting all of them is obtained. Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0162-fourier-entropy-versus-total-influence No independent review

    Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Entropy and singularity of spectral and pivotal sets in planar percolation (arXiv:2609.15388, September 2026) proves that for crossings of critical bond percolation on the square lattice, and of site percolation on the triangular lattice with critical or inhomogeneous near-critical parameters, the Shannon entropies of the spectral sample and of the pivotal set are both comparable to the total influence, of order R^2 alpha_4(R). This answers Question 1 in Section 11 of C. Garban, G. Pete and O. Schramm, The Fourier spectrum of critical percolation (Acta Math. 205, 2010, 19-104), and proves both bounds of Conjecture 8 in G. Kalai, Three puzzles on mathematics, computation, and games (Proc. ICM 2018), for these crossings; the spectral bound is the percolation case of the Friedgut-Kalai Fourier entropy-influence conjecture. For critical triangular-site square crossings the two laws are asymptotically mutually singular. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/percolation-crossing-entropy (commit 29a39246dc9c); ResearchGate record 414266816. Not refereed.

[6] Fourier entropy-influence for linear threshold functions: H(f) <= 14.22 I(f) for every f = sgn(w.x - theta)  (id: claim_fb024fa2ccc6416cacc2948c66e0fd62; claim; score 19.01)

    Every linear threshold function f = sgn(w.x - theta) on {-1,1}^n satisfies H(f) <= 14.22 I(f), where H is the Fourier entropy and I the total influence; the class was listed as open by Chakraborty et al. (LATIN 2018, arXiv:1903.11635). Ranking coordinates by |w_i|, the derivative D_i f is the indicator of a slab of width 2|w_i|, and the Erdos-Littlewood-Offord inequality applied to noise on the heavier coordinates gives E_S sum_{i in S} ln+(r(i)/|S|) <= 4.151 I, so the spectral sample lives on the top O(|S|) coordinates by weight; entropy against a rank-weighted reference measure, plus O'Donnell-Wright-Zhou's level-entropy bound (at most 3I), gives the constant (optimum exponent a = 1.2006, 14.2142). For f = G(w.x) with G changing sign t times, H(f) <= C_t I(f) with C_t = O(log t) (16.57 at t = 2). The supremum of H/I over threshold functions appears numerically to be about 4. The rank criterion is sufficient, not necessary: it fails for recursive ternary majority.

[7] Nearest-point projection onto a C^k hypersurface and the regularity of the distance function  (id: claim_04473831628c7a080682bd877b0c5210827ced36271d2b2a1e05d663ca9c37e2; claim; score 20.15)

    Let S be a compact C^k hypersurface in R^n with k >= 2. Then there is delta > 0 such that on the tubular neighbourhood { x : dist(x, S) < delta } the nearest point of S to x is UNIQUE, the projection map is C^{k-1}, and the signed distance function d is C^k with gradient of unit length equal to the outward normal at the projected point. The largest such delta is governed by the REACH of S, which is bounded below by the reciprocal of the supremum of the principal curvatures and shrinks where the surface nearly self-touches. For a merely C^1 hypersurface the reach can be zero and the projection can fail to be unique arbitrarily close to the surface, so no tubular neighbourhood of uniform width need exist - the standard trap when a proof written for C^2 surfaces is applied to a C^1 one. C^2 (or better) regularity and compactness; the width of the neighbourhood depends on curvature bounds and is not uniform over all surfaces. For a convex set the projection is globally unique and 1-Lipschitz with no curvature hypothesis, which is a different theorem, resting on convexity rather than smoothness.
